screens.title: Client-Server Model in Unreal
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal Engine uses a client-server architecture for multiplayer where the server is the single source of truth. That means physics, game rules, and authoritative state changes are decided on the server; clients send inputs and may locally predict outcomes, but the server ultimately confirms what happened. This separation matters because it prevents inconsistent state and reduces cheating vectors: a server-side check can reject invalid actions. A concrete example is shooting: the client requests to fire by calling a Server RPC; the server validates ammo, hit registration, and then applies damage. A common misconception is that clients can freely change replicated variables — they cannot; replicated variables are driven by server updates unless specifically arranged for client-side prediction with reconciliation. Understanding ownership is essential: only the owning client may call Server RPCs for that actor, and the server can call Client RPCs to notify that owner. When designing gameplay, decide whether logic must be authoritative (server) or can run locally for responsiveness (client prediction). Always plan reconciliation: display immediate feedback locally, but accept server correction. How will you balance responsiveness and authority in your next feature?

keyIdea.title: Server = Source of Truth
keyIdea.text: Server authoritatively updates game state; clients request and predict but must accept server validation.

content.html:
Core Concept
Definition
Client-Server Model
Server is authoritative. Clients send input; server validates and updates state that then replicates back.
  • Clients can predict locally but must accept server corrections.
  • Server-side validation prevents cheating and enforces game rules.
  • Ownership determines who can call which RPCs for a given actor.
Analogy
Think of the server as the referee who makes the final call; players can shout plays but the referee records the official outcome.
Example flow
1. Client -> Server
Client calls a Server RPC with input like 'fire weapon'.
2. Server validation
Server checks ammo, hit validity, then applies authoritative damage.
3. Server -> Clients
Server replicates state changes or calls NetMulticast to show visuals across all clients.
Key Takeaway

Plan authority first. Authoritative actions live on the server; visuals and immediate response can be handled locally but must accept corrections.

screens.title: Replication: Synchronizing Game State
screens.narratorSegment: Replication is the process by which the server's authoritative state is propagated to connected clients. It covers variable values, object properties, and function calls, ensuring everyone sees the same world. In Unreal Engine you explicitly mark what should replicate. For variables you commonly use the UPROPERTY(Replicated) specifier; for functions you declare RPCs that run on remote machines. But marking a variable alone isn't sufficient: you must register it in GetLifetimeReplicatedProps using DOREPLIFETIME so the engine knows to send updates and under what conditions. Replication can be optimized with conditions like owner-only or spatial relevancy to avoid wasting bandwidth on irrelevant updates. A practical example is a player's health: replicate it so other players see damage, but you might choose COND_OwnerOnly if only the owner needs sensitive details. A frequent misconception is that replication sends every change instantly and cheaply; in reality it consumes network bandwidth and must be designed with update frequency and conditions in mind. Consider whether a property needs to be authoritative and how often it changes before you replicate it. Replication: Synchronizing Game State means explicitly mark what the server should send and register it so the engine can synchronize state efficiently.. In practical terms, how replication keeps clients up to date and what you must mark. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Replication fundamentals
What replicates
  • Variables marked with UPROPERTY(Replicated) or ReplicatedUsing.
  • RPC calls declared with UFUNCTION(Server/Client/NetMulticast).
  • Actor and component state when bReplicates is true.
Optimization
Use replication conditions to limit who receives updates and when.
Concrete example
Health replication pattern
1) Mark CurrentHealth with UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_CurrentHealth).
2) Register it in GetLifetimeReplicatedProps using DOREPLIFETIME.
3) Update health on server and let clients react in OnRep.
Key Takeaway

Replication is explicit. Mark and register properties, then choose conditions that balance bandwidth and gameplay needs.

screens.title: UPROPERTY(Replicated) and OnRep Functions
screens.narratorSegment: When a variable must be synchronized from server to clients, the common pattern is to declare it with a replication specifier and optionally an OnRep callback. For example, using UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_CurrentHealth) tells the engine to run OnRep_CurrentHealth on clients when the replicated value changes. On the server you modify the variable; the engine then serializes and sends the new value to relevant clients according to the lifetime registration. A practical example: you change CurrentHealth on the server, then clients receive the update and OnRep_CurrentHealth can update local UI or play effects. A misconception is that OnRep provides the previous value automatically; it provides the new value, so if you need a delta you must store the old value locally before applying changes on the server or compute it inside the server call and replicate that information as needed. Remember that OnRep runs only on clients, not on the server version of the object. Use these callbacks to update HUD elements, local sound, or animations in a safe, non-authoritative way. UPROPERTY(Replicated) and OnRep Functions means use replicatedusing to run client-side handlers when the server changes a replicated value.. In practical terms, marking properties and reacting to updates on clients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: OnRep callback
keyIdea.text: Use ReplicatedUsing to run client-side handlers when the server changes a replicated value.

content.html:
Process Flow
Code walkthrough
Code example
This snippet shows the property and OnRep declaration.
// Header excerpt
UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_CurrentHealth, VisibleAnywhere, Category = "Health")
float CurrentHealth;

UFUNCTION()
void OnRep_CurrentHealth();
Notes and example actions
  • Change CurrentHealth only on the server. Clients receive updates via replication.
  • OnRep_CurrentHealth runs on clients — update HUD or play local VFX there.
  • If you need the change delta, calculate it server-side and replicate that value too, or cache previous value locally.
Common mistake
Forgetting that OnRep does not run on the server build of the actor — server-side logic must be handled where the change originates.
Key Takeaway

Use ReplicatedUsing for client-side reactions, compute deltas consciously, and never rely on OnRep for server-side authoritative work.

screens.title: GetLifetimeReplicatedProps & DOREPLIFETIME
screens.narratorSegment: Marking a property with a replication specifier alone does not inform the engine how to treat it at runtime. You must override GetLifetimeReplicatedProps in your actor or component and call DOREPLIFETIME using your class and property names. This function is where you register properties and optionally specify replication conditions like owner-only replication. For example, calling DOREPLIFETIME(UMyHealthComponent, CurrentHealth) registers that variable for replication. You can also use DOREPLIFETIME_CONDITION to only send a property to the owning client, which is useful for private data. A common mistake is omitting this registration and expecting replication to happen anyway. Another nuance: perform registration in the component or actor that actually holds the variable; if a component owns a variable, its GetLifetimeReplicatedProps must register it. Testing requires running a server and client instance and observing that values change and OnRep handlers fire on clients after server changes. This registration step is small but essential: it makes replication explicit and controllable. GetLifetimeReplicatedProps & DOREPLIFETIME means override getlifetimereplicatedprops and use doreplifetime to enable replication for each property.. In practical terms, register properties so the engine knows what to send. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Override GetLifetimeReplicatedProps and use DOREPLIFETIME to enable replication for each property.

content.html:
Definition
GetLifetimeReplicatedProps
Code example
// CPP excerpt
void UMyHealthComponent::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps(TArray& OutLifetimeProps) const
{
  Super::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps(OutLifetimeProps);
  DOREPLIFETIME(UMyHealthComponent, CurrentHealth);
  // DOREPLIFETIME_CONDITION(UMyHealthComponent, Inventory, COND_OwnerOnly);
}
Practical notes
  • Always call Super::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps first.
  • Use DOREPLIFETIME for straightforward replication and DOREPLIFETIME_CONDITION to control recipients.
  • Register properties in the class that owns them — components must register component properties.
Common mistake
Forgetting to register properties leads to no replication even if UPROPERTY declares Replicated.
Key Takeaway

GetLifetimeReplicatedProps is where replication becomes active; register every replicated property there.

screens.title: Replication Conditions & Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Replication is powerful, but it uses network bandwidth. Unreal provides replication conditions to control who receives which updates. For example, COND_OwnerOnly limits a property to the owning client, preventing other players from seeing private data. COND_SkipOwner excludes the owner but sends to others. Conditions are useful for inventory or private stats where only the owner needs full detail. Another optimization is to reduce frequency or only replicate when values change significantly. A typical case: positional updates for distant actors can be sent less frequently or when within relevancy range. Misconceptions here include assuming all properties should be global; instead, ask: who needs this value, and how often? When you must show a visual effect to everyone, prefer NetMulticast RPCs for events, but use replicated state for persistent properties. Designing replication with conditions preserves bandwidth and prevents accidental information leaks. Think critically about each replicated field and choose the narrowest condition that satisfies gameplay. keyIdea.title: Optimize replication
keyIdea.text: Use replication conditions and relevancy to reduce bandwidth and avoid leaking private data.

content.html:
Comparison
Conditions & use cases
COND_OwnerOnly
Only the actor owner receives the update. Good for private HUD data or inventory details.
COND_SkipOwner
Sends to everyone except the owner. Useful for mirrored visuals where owner handles local effect differently.
Spatial relevancy
Only replicate actors near a client or within relevancy ranges to limit traffic for distant objects.
Practical checklist
  • Ask: who needs this value? Only owner, all clients, or server-only?
  • Choose a condition, or avoid replication for frequently changing non-critical values.
  • Use NetMulticast for one-time global events, not for high-frequency state.
Key Takeaway

Prefer narrow replication conditions and event RPCs to preserve bandwidth and protect private data.

screens.title: RPC Types: Server, Client, NetMulticast
screens.narratorSegment: Remote Procedure Calls route function execution between client and server. There are three primary types in Unreal: Server, Client, and NetMulticast. A Server RPC is called by a client and executed on the server — it is used for authoritative actions like firing a weapon or attempting to pick up an item. It often requires Reliable delivery and WithValidation so the server can reject invalid requests. A Client RPC is called by the server and runs only on the owning client; use it to trigger client-specific UI or audio. NetMulticast RPCs are called by the server and execute on all clients, so they are ideal for global visual effects like explosions. A common mistake is attempting to call a Server RPC from a client that does not own the target actor — that call will fail silently. Another pitfall is calling Client RPCs from a client; only the server should invoke them. Always reason about origin: who initiates the action, who must authoritatively decide it, and who needs to be informed as a result. This mental model keeps RPCs correct and predictable.

keyIdea.title: RPC routing
keyIdea.text: Server: client->server; Client: server->specific client; NetMulticast: server->all clients.

content.html:
Core Concept
RPC comparison
Server RPC
Called by client, executed on server. Use for authoritative actions and validate inputs.
Example: Server_AttemptPickup() verifies item availability and updates inventory.
Client RPC
Called by server, executed on a specific owning client. Use for owner-only UI notifications.
Example: Client_DisplayHitMarker() shows a hit marker only to the shooter.
NetMulticast RPC
Called by server, executed on all clients. Use for global visuals and sounds.
Example: Multicast_PlayExplosionEffect() so everyone sees the explosion.
Practical warning
RPCs must be called from the correct authority and origin. Verify ownership before calling a Server RPC and never call client-only RPCs from clients.

screens.title: Server RPCs: Validation and Authority
screens.narratorSegment: Server RPCs must be implemented with an awareness of authority and potential abuse. A client calls a Server RPC to request an authoritative action; the server then runs validation logic if appropriate and finally performs the action. The common UFUNCTION declaration includes Server, Reliable, and WithValidation. The WithValidation pattern generates a separate _Validate function where you check whether the request is allowed — for example whether the player has enough ammo or is in range. The _Implementation function becomes the authoritative code path that actually changes game state. A frequent misconception is that Reliable means instant; it only guarantees delivery, not immediacy. For high-frequency inputs like fine-grained movement, Unreal uses specialized movement replication. Also, clients may only call Server RPCs on actors they own; enforce ownership checks to avoid unexpected failures. When implementing Server RPCs, structure your code to validate first, then apply changes, then replicate resulting state or call NetMulticast for global events. This order keeps actions secure and consistent across instances. Server RPCs: Validation and Authority means validate client requests, then perform authoritative updates on the server; use reliable when delivery matters.. In practical terms, how to write server rpcs with validation and correct ownership checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Client RPCs & NetMulticast Details
screens.narratorSegment: Client RPCs and NetMulticast RPCs both originate on the server, but they target different recipients. Use a Client RPC when the server needs to notify exactly one owning client about a private event, like showing a damage HUD or playing a local sound. The server calls the Client RPC and it executes on the owning client's machine only. NetMulticast is for events that should be visible to everyone: the server calls a NetMulticast RPC and it executes on all connected clients and the server itself in a listen-server setup. A common pitfall is using NetMulticast for owner-only visuals or trying to call a Client RPC from a client. Also, keep NetMulticast calls lightweight because they run on all machines. When you need persistent replicated state plus a one-time visual, combine replication for state and NetMulticast for immediate effects. Always reason about who needs the information and choose the narrower RPC when possible to avoid unnecessary network work. Client vs Multicast
Client RPC
Server calls a function that executes only on the owning client. Good for private UI updates.

screens.title: bReplicates and Actor/Component Setup
screens.narratorSegment: For replication to work, the actor or component that holds replicated data must be configured to replicate. This is often as simple as setting bReplicates = true in the actor or component constructor. For components, mark the component as replicating and ensure the owner actor also allows replication. Hands-on Lab
Live coding steps
Starter/Reference code
// MyHealthComponent.h (excerpt)
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "Components/ActorComponent.h"
#include "Net/UnrealNetwork.h"
#include "MyHealthComponent.generated.h"

DECLARE_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_TwoParams(FOnHealthChanged, float, float);

UCLASS( ClassGroup=(Custom), meta=(BlueprintSpawnableComponent) )
class YOURGAME_API UMyHealthComponent : public UActorComponent
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UMyHealthComponent();

protected:
    virtual void BeginPlay() override;
    virtual void GetLifetimeReplicatedProps(TArray& OutLifetimeProps) const override;

public:
    UFUNCTION(Server, Reliable, WithValidation)
    void Server_ApplyDamage(float DamageAmount);
    bool Server_ApplyDamage_Validate(float DamageAmount);
    void Server_ApplyDamage_Implementation(float DamageAmount);

    UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_CurrentHealth, VisibleAnywhere, Category = "Health")
    float CurrentHealth;

    UFUNCTION()
    void OnRep_CurrentHealth();

    UPROPERTY(EditDefaultsOnly, Category = "Health")
    float MaxHealth = 100.0f;

    FOnHealthChanged OnHealthChanged;

    UFUNCTION(NetMulticast, Reliable)
    void Multicast_PlayDamageEffect();
    void Multicast_PlayDamageEffect_Implementation();
};
Step checklist & testing
  1. In constructor: set bReplicates = true and CurrentHealth = MaxHealth.
  2. Implement GetLifetimeReplicatedProps calling DOREPLIFETIME(UMyHealthComponent, CurrentHealth).
  3. Implement Server_ApplyDamage_Validate to return true and _Implementation to reduce, clamp, and call Multicast_PlayDamageEffect().
  4. Implement OnRep_CurrentHealth to broadcast or log the update on clients.
  5. Implement Multicast_PlayDamageEffect_Implementation to log or spawn an effect visible on all clients.
  6. Set owning actor's bReplicates = true and call Server_ApplyDamage from client input. Test with two instances and watch logs.
Testing tip
Run one editor instance as server and a second as client. Use UE_LOG to observe OnRep firing on the client and multicast logs on both sides.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will build a practical understanding of multiplayer in Unreal Engine. You will learn the client-server model that gives the server authoritative control, why replication is the mechanism that keeps clients synchronized, and how Remote Procedure Calls let code run on the right machine. We'll focus on concrete, testable patterns: marking properties with replication specifiers, implementing GetLifetimeReplicatedProps with DOREPLIFETIME, using Server, Client, and NetMulticast RPCs correctly, and common debugging steps. For a hands-on outcome you'll extend a health component so damage replicates and a multicast effect plays across all players. This matters because multiplayer code must balance authority, bandwidth, and responsiveness: get the architecture right and you prevent cheating and desyncs; get it wrong and gameplay breaks or leaks private data. As we go, pay attention to ownership rules and replication conditions — these are the details that make networking predictable. By the end you'll be able to decide where logic should run, mark the right properties for replication, and implement basic RPCs that follow Unreal's authority model.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to read and reason about Unreal's client-server model, and make practical replication decisions in C++ code. You'll explain why the server must be authoritative and how clients send inputs that the server validates and applies. You will mark properties for replication using the appropriate UPROPERTY specifiers and implement GetLifetimeReplicatedProps so the engine knows what to replicate. You will also identify when to use replication conditions like owner-only to reduce bandwidth or to hide private data. These skills matter because multiplayer games need predictable authority and efficient bandwidth usage to remain synchronized and fair. For example, you will be able to set up a health variable to replicate only to the owning client or to all clients depending on gameplay needs, and justify that choice. The learning here combines concept and action: knowing the theory and making the code changes that enforce it.

These objectives focus on implementation and testing. You will implement Server and NetMulticast RPCs, understand Reliable vs. Unreliable choices, and add validation where appropriate. You'll know when to mark a component or actor as replicating and how to test using two editor instances so you can observe replication and log messages on both server and client. You will also learn troubleshooting patterns: checking ownership, verifying bReplicates is set, ensuring GetLifetimeReplicatedProps includes each replicated property, and confirming OnRep functions fire on clients. These practices matter because many networking bugs are not obvious until you run separate instances and inspect role and log output. For example, you'll set bReplicates to true in a component and then observe that OnRep_CurrentHealth fires on the client when the server adjusts health. The combined goal is to leave you able to both write replication code and verify it in a real test setup.

Unreal Engine uses a client-server architecture for multiplayer where the server is the single source of truth. That means physics, game rules, and authoritative state changes are decided on the server; clients send inputs and may locally predict outcomes, but the server ultimately confirms what happened. This separation matters because it prevents inconsistent state and reduces cheating vectors: a server-side check can reject invalid actions. A concrete example is shooting: the client requests to fire by calling a Server RPC; the server validates ammo, hit registration, and then applies damage. A common misconception is that clients can freely change replicated variables — they cannot; replicated variables are driven by server updates unless specifically arranged for client-side prediction with reconciliation. Understanding ownership is essential: only the owning client may call Server RPCs for that actor, and the server can call Client RPCs to notify that owner. When designing gameplay, decide whether logic must be authoritative (server) or can run locally for responsiveness (client prediction). Always plan reconciliation: display immediate feedback locally, but accept server correction. How will you balance responsiveness and authority in your next feature?

Replication is the process by which the server's authoritative state is propagated to connected clients. It covers variable values, object properties, and function calls, ensuring everyone sees the same world. In Unreal Engine you explicitly mark what should replicate. For variables you commonly use the UPROPERTY(Replicated) specifier; for functions you declare RPCs that run on remote machines. But marking a variable alone isn't sufficient: you must register it in GetLifetimeReplicatedProps using DOREPLIFETIME so the engine knows to send updates and under what conditions. Replication can be optimized with conditions like owner-only or spatial relevancy to avoid wasting bandwidth on irrelevant updates. A practical example is a player's health: replicate it so other players see damage, but you might choose COND_OwnerOnly if only the owner needs sensitive details. A frequent misconception is that replication sends every change instantly and cheaply; in reality it consumes network bandwidth and must be designed with update frequency and conditions in mind. Consider whether a property needs to be authoritative and how often it changes before you replicate it. Replication: Synchronizing Game State means explicitly mark what the server should send and register it so the engine can synchronize state efficiently.. In practical terms, how replication keeps clients up to date and what you must mark. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a variable must be synchronized from server to clients, the common pattern is to declare it with a replication specifier and optionally an OnRep callback. For example, using UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_CurrentHealth) tells the engine to run OnRep_CurrentHealth on clients when the replicated value changes. On the server you modify the variable; the engine then serializes and sends the new value to relevant clients according to the lifetime registration. A practical example: you change CurrentHealth on the server, then clients receive the update and OnRep_CurrentHealth can update local UI or play effects. A misconception is that OnRep provides the previous value automatically; it provides the new value, so if you need a delta you must store the old value locally before applying changes on the server or compute it inside the server call and replicate that information as needed. Remember that OnRep runs only on clients, not on the server version of the object. Use these callbacks to update HUD elements, local sound, or animations in a safe, non-authoritative way. UPROPERTY(Replicated) and OnRep Functions means use replicatedusing to run client-side handlers when the server changes a replicated value.. In practical terms, marking properties and reacting to updates on clients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Marking a property with a replication specifier alone does not inform the engine how to treat it at runtime. You must override GetLifetimeReplicatedProps in your actor or component and call DOREPLIFETIME using your class and property names. This function is where you register properties and optionally specify replication conditions like owner-only replication. For example, calling DOREPLIFETIME(UMyHealthComponent, CurrentHealth) registers that variable for replication. You can also use DOREPLIFETIME_CONDITION to only send a property to the owning client, which is useful for private data. A common mistake is omitting this registration and expecting replication to happen anyway. Another nuance: perform registration in the component or actor that actually holds the variable; if a component owns a variable, its GetLifetimeReplicatedProps must register it. Testing requires running a server and client instance and observing that values change and OnRep handlers fire on clients after server changes. This registration step is small but essential: it makes replication explicit and controllable. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Replication is powerful, but it uses network bandwidth. Unreal provides replication conditions to control who receives which updates. For example, COND_OwnerOnly limits a property to the owning client, preventing other players from seeing private data. COND_SkipOwner excludes the owner but sends to others. Conditions are useful for inventory or private stats where only the owner needs full detail. Another optimization is to reduce frequency or only replicate when values change significantly. A typical case: positional updates for distant actors can be sent less frequently or when within relevancy range. Misconceptions here include assuming all properties should be global; instead, ask: who needs this value, and how often? When you must show a visual effect to everyone, prefer NetMulticast RPCs for events, but use replicated state for persistent properties. Designing replication with conditions preserves bandwidth and prevents accidental information leaks. Think critically about each replicated field and choose the narrowest condition that satisfies gameplay. Remote Procedure Calls route function execution between client and server. There are three primary types in Unreal: Server, Client, and NetMulticast. A Server RPC is called by a client and executed on the server — it is used for authoritative actions like firing a weapon or attempting to pick up an item. It often requires Reliable delivery and WithValidation so the server can reject invalid requests. A Client RPC is called by the server and runs only on the owning client; use it to trigger client-specific UI or audio. NetMulticast RPCs are called by the server and execute on all clients, so they are ideal for global visual effects like explosions. A common mistake is attempting to call a Server RPC from a client that does not own the target actor — that call will fail silently. Another pitfall is calling Client RPCs from a client; only the server should invoke them. Always reason about origin: who initiates the action, who must authoritatively decide it, and who needs to be informed as a result. This mental model keeps RPCs correct and predictable.

Server RPCs must be implemented with an awareness of authority and potential abuse. A client calls a Server RPC to request an authoritative action; the server then runs validation logic if appropriate and finally performs the action. The common UFUNCTION declaration includes Server, Reliable, and WithValidation. The WithValidation pattern generates a separate _Validate function where you check whether the request is allowed — for example whether the player has enough ammo or is in range. The _Implementation function becomes the authoritative code path that actually changes game state. A frequent misconception is that Reliable means instant; it only guarantees delivery, not immediacy. For high-frequency inputs like fine-grained movement, Unreal uses specialized movement replication. Also, clients may only call Server RPCs on actors they own; enforce ownership checks to avoid unexpected failures. This order keeps actions secure and consistent across instances.
